ABSTRACT

WEB-BASED MAPPING AND ASSESSMENT OF THE SPATIAL EXTENT, INTENSITY AND RESILIENCE OF FLOOD IN LUGBE, ABUJA, NIGERIA

Journal: Environment & Ecosystem Science (EES)

Author:Innocent E. Bello, Nancy B. Madugu, Hadiza A. Zaku, Abubakar U. Tafida

This is an open access article distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution License CC BY 4.0, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited

DOI: 10.26480/ees.02.2026.121.124

This study assessed the spatial extent and intensity of flooding in Lugbe, Abuja, using integrated geospatial techniques and rainfall–flood relationship modeling to inform sustainable flood risk management and urban planning. An interdisciplinary approach combining Remote Sensing, Geographic Information Systems (GIS), hydrological modeling, and WebGIS visualization was applied to delineate flood-prone zones, assess hazard intensity, and examine governance implications. The findings indicate that flooding is highly concentrated in low-lying drainage corridors and rapidly urbanizing areas, notably Trademore Estate, the Voice of Nigeria axis, River Park Estate, and informal settlements near the Lugbe Fruit Market. Flood intensity varies across locations, with relatively low exposure in FHA Capua (1.59 ha; 1.39%) and high-intensity hotspots in River Park (21.5 ha; 4.48%). Overall, about 34% of Lugbe lies within moderate-to-high flood hazard zones, with severe areas experiencing flood depths exceeding 1.5 m. Spatial analysis further reveals that approximately 33–36% of buildings and road networks are exposed to flood risk. High impervious surface coverage (65–75%) and blocked or undersized drainage systems affecting nearly 40% of mapped corridors significantly exacerbate runoff accumulation. Rainfall modeling shows that extreme rainfall events (>50 mm/day) contribute to over 60% of severe flooding, while a 10% increase in rainfall intensity could raise runoff volumes by 15–20%. The integration of WebGIS dashboards improves hazard communication by 40–50% and reduces response time by up to 45%, enhancing flood governance. The study recommends improved drainage maintenance, strict land-use enforcement, and the protection of natural waterways.
